title: US households kept their inflation medians steady as perceived payment risk rose
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: The New York Fed’s October Survey of Consumer Expectations found unchanged median inflation expectations at all three horizons, alongside a rise in the perceived risk of missing a debt payment. Households also became more pessimistic about the national unemployment rate, yet a worker who imagined losing a job was slightly more confident of finding another one. The combination matters for reading US demand. An aggregate deterioration in labour sentiment can coexist with relatively steady expectations for income and spending and a more concentrated concern about financial resilience. These conclusions describe households’ answers collected on 1–31 October, released on 9 November. They are neither forecasts by the New York Fed nor observations of actual defaults or job losses.

In the inflation section, the median stood at 3.9% one year ahead, 3.3% three years ahead and 3.0% five years ahead. Stability at the median concealed changes in both the distribution of answers and respondents’ own confidence. The distance between the 75th and 25th percentiles narrowed at one and five years and was unchanged at three years. Median individual uncertainty fell at one and three years and was steady at five. Those are different statistics: respondents may agree more closely with one another without each becoming more certain about future prices. Nor did a stable overall median mean stable expectations about each household expense. The expected year-ahead increase in petrol prices dropped 0.6 percentage point to 4.2%, while the corresponding rent figure rose 0.9 point to 7.7%. The release does not aggregate those category changes into contributions to the overall median.

The labour section distinguishes three probabilities. The mean probability attached to the national unemployment rate being higher a year ahead rose 1.4 percentage points to 45.3%, the highest since April 2020. Respondents without a college degree drove the increase. The mean perceived probability of personally losing a job rose 0.4 point to 13.9%, still below its trailing twelve-month average. Conversely, the mean probability of finding a job conditional on losing the current one increased to 46.5%, its highest since November 2025. Expectations of voluntary quits edged down, while median expected earnings growth remained 2.6%. A probability of national unemployment rising does not measure its expected level, and an improving conditional job-finding assessment need not cancel a rise in the perceived risk of job loss.

In household finance, the median expected growth of household income slipped to 3.0%, within the narrow range observed since June 2025. Median expected spending growth declined to 5.3%, still above its twelve-month average. By contrast, the mean perceived probability of missing a minimum debt payment over the next three months jumped 1.6 percentage points to 13.8%, the highest since December 2025. Assessments of current and future credit access changed little. Slightly more favourable evaluations of households’ finances compared with a year earlier also coexisted with broadly unchanged assessments of their situation a year ahead.

The survey draws on a nationally representative rotating internet panel of about 1,300 household heads, who can remain in it for up to twelve months. That design permits investigation of whether the same households report several pressures together. The release presents aggregates and does not establish that the people forecasting missed payments were those reporting weaker employment prospects. For a credit or consumption view, that missing link matters more than a simple subtraction of median spending growth from median income growth. Such an arithmetic difference would mix separate distributions and would not measure any household’s cash shortfall.

questions.question: Is the rise in missed-payment risk concentrated among the households reporting greater job insecurity?
questions.detail: The release identifies a rise in each perceived probability but gives no joint distribution. A shared group of exposed borrowers would have different implications for consumer credit than two unrelated changes. Use the rotating SCE panel and the questionnaire cited in the release to compare within-household changes, controlling for panel entry and exit; examine income and education groups separately.

questions.question: Which households account for the divergence between expected rent and petrol inflation?
questions.detail: Both category expectations moved appreciably while the overall inflation median was stable. The aggregate survey cannot show how a given household weights its costs or why its expectations changed. For inflation-risk analysis, examine household-level answers, dispersion and housing status across consecutive waves. Compare the wording and horizons in the SCE questionnaire before matching its category expectations to official price components.

questions.question: How closely do subjective delinquency risks lead realised credit outcomes?
questions.detail: The reported three-month probability rose even though perceptions of credit access barely moved. To translate this into expected losses, compare historical survey probabilities at the same horizon with subsequent delinquency transitions in official household-credit data. Check for changes in borrower mix and product coverage. A calibration based on the share of debts delinquent would measure something different from a household’s risk of missing a minimum payment.
